title: Validating Input and Reporting Errors
summary: Check every request at the edge, decide between 400, 409, and 422, and answer every error in one Problem Details format.
intro: Everything a client sends is just text, and some of it is wrong: a typo, a phone app two versions behind, a script written in a hurry, and now and then a person poking for weaknesses. An API that trusts what arrives ends up storing a booking for minus five people, crashing on a date it can't read, or answering with an error so vague nobody can fix their request. This lesson shows you how to check every request where it enters, with a schema for each body and query string, where each kind of check belongs, and which status code each failure earns. Then it gives every error one shape, the Problem Details format, built in one central place in Go.

steps.title: Never trust input
steps.body:
Your server can't see who is on the other end. A request from Roombook's own web app looks just like one typed into curl, and anyone can type into curl. So every part of a request, its path, query string, headers, and body, is input from outside, and could be anything at all. It goes wrong in two ways:

- **Wrong by mistake**: a misspelled field, a date in the wrong format, a number sent as text, an end time before the start, or a client built against last year's version of the API.
- **Hostile on purpose**: a fifty-megabyte body, a note of a million characters, an id of `-1` or `99999999999999999999`, or a field nobody should be able to set, like `"isAdmin": true`, or `"status": "confirmed"` on a booking that broke the rules.

## Parse at the edge

The answer is to check everything in one place: the **edge** of your API, where requests come in, before any of your own code uses them. Picture a line drawn around your server's code, called the **trust boundary**. Outside the line is text from strangers. Inside are values your code can rely on.

```diagram validation-and-errors-trust
Text from outside is checked once, at the boundary, and only typed values go further in.
```

Crossing the line is the job of **parsing**: turning text into typed values, or refusing. A parser for a booking doesn't just answer yes or no. It hands back a booking whose `attendees` is a whole number from 1 to 30, whose times are real moments in UTC, and which has no fields nobody expected. Code inside the line takes that value and never checks those things again. The idea has a slogan: **parse, don't validate**. Checking the text and then passing the text on leaves every later function wondering whether it was checked. Passing on the parsed value makes the checking part of the type.

A **schema** is how you describe a valid input: each field, its type, whether it's required, and its limits. A schema library reads a request against it and gives back either the typed value or a list of everything that's wrong.

## Why Go's types aren't enough

Go's types do check something at run time. `encoding/json` won't put `"lots"` into an `int`. But a type only says what kind of value fits, not which values make sense. `-5` is a perfectly good `int`, and an end time an hour before the start is a perfectly good `time.Time`. A missing field is quietly left at its zero value, so `0` and absent look the same. And by default, a field the struct doesn't have, like `isAdmin`, is dropped without a word. The example shows a struct with no checks taking all of that.

Go has no schema library in its standard library, and Roombook doesn't need one. Each request type gets a hand-written `validate` method that checks every field and returns the parsed value, which part 2 writes. `go-playground/validator`, which reads checks from struct tags, is a popular package if you'd rather not write them by hand.

examples.title: A handler that trusts its input
examples.prompt: This handler decodes the body into a struct with no checks, and answers `201` with the struct. Send it a booking that breaks every rule.
examples.explanation: `encoding/json` read every value into the struct's types without complaint, and the handler answered 201. The booking ends an hour before it starts, has minus five people, and `isAdmin` vanished, since the struct has no such field. Send `"attendees": "lots"` instead, and decoding does fail, so the types catch mistakes in the format, but none in the rules. A real handler would now store this booking, and the bug would surface later, far from its cause. The fix is a `validate` method that every request goes through before the handler uses it.

steps.title: Schemas for request bodies

examples.title: Normalized on the way in
examples.prompt: Book Turing with a start time two hours ahead of UTC, and a note with spaces around it.
examples.code: curl -s localhost:8080/v1/bookings -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"roomId": 1, "startsAt": "2026-10-05T16:00:00+02:00", "endsAt": "2026-10-05T15:30:00Z", "attendees": 3, "note": "  Algorithms study group  "}'
examples.explanation: The request said `16:00:00+02:00`, and the stored booking says `14:00:00Z`: the same moment, now in UTC, so every later comparison, like checking for overlaps, compares like with like. The spaces around the note are gone. The rest of the booking comes from the service and the store, which the next lesson builds: an id, the user, a status, a version, and when it was created, which is the course's fixed clock. None of those were the client's to set, and the schema made sure they weren't.

examples.title: Several mistakes, one answer
examples.prompt: Send a booking with several things wrong at once.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/validation-failed","title":"Validation failed","status":422,"detail":"3 fields are invalid.","instance":"/v1/bookings","requestId":"3BRJHEFTP6RGANFOQH2X7K4ME3","errors":[{"field":"roomId","message":"must be a positive whole number"},{"field":"startsAt","message":"must be a time like 2026-10-05T14:00:00Z"},{"field":"attendees","message":"must be between 1 and 30"}]}
examples.explanation: This body decodes cleanly, so `validate` ran and reported all three problems at once: the room id is 0, the start time isn't a time, and there are no attendees. The messages are Roombook's own, written once in `validate`. Send `"roomId": "1"` instead, and you get a 400 `invalid-json` problem, because decoding stops at a value it can't convert and `validate` never runs. The rule comparing the two times didn't run either, since `startsAt` didn't parse. The shape of the whole answer is part 5's subject.

steps.title: Path, query, and header values

examples.title: A query string with three mistakes
examples.prompt: Ask for rooms with a capacity that isn't a number, a limit over the maximum, and a made-up cursor.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/validation-failed","title":"Validation failed","status":422,"detail":"3 fields are invalid.","instance":"/v1/rooms","requestId":"6UNS2FAQ6YVFUGXZNY7XNZG5EE","errors":[{"field":"minCapacity","message":"must be a whole number"},{"field":"limit","message":"must be between 1 and 100"},{"field":"cursor","message":"is not a cursor this API issued"}]}
examples.explanation: All three problems come back at once: `lots` isn't a whole number, `500` is over the limit, and `abc` isn't a cursor the API made. The messages are Roombook's own, from `parseRoomQuery`. The answer is the same shape as the body errors in part 2, so a client handles both with the same code. Ask for `minCapacity=5&limit=1` instead, and you get Hopper alone, the first by name of the two rooms that seat five or more, with a `nextCursor` for the next page.

examples.title: An id that names nothing
examples.prompt: Ask for a booking whose id isn't a number.
examples.explanation: A path that can't name a booking is a 404, the same answer as a booking id that's a number but doesn't exist. To the client, both mean there's nothing at that URL, so there's no reason to tell them apart, and no reason to say how ids are checked. The `type` is Roombook's `not-found` problem, the same for every 404.

steps.title: Where each check belongs

examples.title: Three broken rules
examples.prompt: Book Lovelace, which holds four, for five people, starting at a quarter past and lasting three and three quarter hours.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/validation-failed","title":"Validation failed","status":422,"detail":"3 fields are invalid.","instance":"/v1/bookings","requestId":"GICT5V4HOV4ND7FBFENQIJWWWN","errors":[{"field":"startsAt","message":"must be on the hour or half past"},{"field":"endsAt","message":"a booking lasts 30 minutes to 3 hours"},{"field":"attendees","message":"Lovelace holds at most 4 people"}]}
examples.explanation: The body passed the schema: every field had the right type and range. Then the service found three broken rules and reported all of them, in the same shape as the schema's errors: the start isn't on the hour or half past, the booking is longer than three hours, and Lovelace holds four. It's a 422, since this request is wrong no matter what anyone else has booked. Only the request can be fixed, and the messages say exactly what to change.

examples.title: A booking that clashes
examples.prompt: With Ada's 14:00 to 15:30 booking of Turing already made, book Turing from 15:00 to 16:00.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/booking-overlap","title":"Room already booked","status":409,"detail":"The room is already booked then.","instance":"/v1/bookings","requestId":"63IRUZE2EX5RTL7B4OY7MUP34U"}
examples.explanation: Every field and every rule was fine, so the request reached the store, which found the overlap with the existing booking and refused. It's a 409, with its own type, `booking-overlap`, so a client can tell it apart from every other conflict and offer to show the room's free times. The same request succeeds once the other booking is cancelled, which is what makes it a conflict and not a 422. Once the lesson on constraints and transactions moves the check into the database, the answer stays exactly the same.

steps.title: One error format: Problem Details
steps.body:
Clients have to understand your errors as well as your successes. A web app wants to show each message beside the right form field, a script wants to know whether trying again could help, and a developer wants enough to fix their request. If each endpoint invents its own error shape, every client writes special cases for each one. Roombook uses one shape for every error, the **Problem Details** format from RFC 9457, which the lesson on what an API is introduced.

## The standard members

A problem is a JSON object sent with the media type `application/problem+json`, so a client can tell an error body from a normal one by its `Content-Type` alone. RFC 9457 defines five members, all optional:

| Member | Holds | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | A URI that names the kind of problem | `https://roombook.example/problems/booking-overlap` |
| `title` | A short summary of that kind, the same every time | `Room already booked` |
| `status` | The HTTP status code, repeated in the body | `409` |
| `detail` | What went wrong this time, for a person to read | `The room is already booked then.` |
| `instance` | Which occurrence it was. Roombook uses the request's path | `/v1/bookings` |

`type` is the member clients act on. Code compares the type, never the words in `title` or `detail`, which you're free to reword. So a type URI, once published, keeps its meaning for good. It doesn't have to load anything, but a page there that explains the problem is good manners. When a problem has no `type`, the RFC says to read it as `about:blank`, which means nothing beyond the status code. Roombook gives every problem a type of its own instead, so a client can always switch on `type` and never needs a fallback.

## Roombook's problem types

| `type`, after `https://roombook.example/problems/` | Status | `title` |
|---|---|---|
| `invalid-json` | 400 | Body is not valid JSON |
| `not-found` | 404 | Resource not found |
| `method-not-allowed` | 405 | Method not allowed |
| `body-too-large` | 413 | Request body too large |
| `unsupported-media-type` | 415 | Unsupported media type |
| `validation-failed` | 422 | Validation failed |
| `room-not-found` | 422 | Room not found |
| `booking-overlap` | 409 | Room already booked |
| `booking-limit` | 409 | Too many upcoming bookings |
| `internal-error` | 500 | Internal server error |

The database lessons add `room-name-taken`, `email-taken`, and `stale-booking`, and the lesson on passwords and sessions adds the authentication problems, always under the same address.

## Two members of Roombook's own

The RFC lets you add members of your own, called **extension members**, and Roombook adds two:

- `requestId`, the id from the middleware lesson, on every problem, so a user can quote it and you can find the request's log lines.
- `errors`, on `validation-failed`, a list with one entry per broken field: `field`, the field's path, and `message`. A path names a field the way you'd reach it in the JSON, like `endsAt`, or `items.0.name` for a field inside a list.

Always report every field error at once. A form with three mistakes should get one answer with three errors, not three round trips that each reveal one more.

Here is how Roombook builds problems, in `internal/api/problems.go`:

```go
var titles = map[string]string{
	"invalid-json":           "Body is not valid JSON",
	"not-found":              "Resource not found",
	"method-not-allowed":     "Method not allowed",
	"body-too-large":         "Request body too large",
	"unsupported-media-type": "Unsupported media type",
	"validation-failed":      "Validation failed",
	"room-not-found":         "Room not found",
	"booking-overlap":        "Room already booked",
	"booking-limit":          "Too many upcoming bookings",
	"internal-error":         "Internal server error",
}

var byStatus = map[int]string{
	http.StatusBadRequest:            "invalid-json",
	http.StatusNotFound:              "not-found",
	http.StatusMethodNotAllowed:      "method-not-allowed",
	http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge: "body-too-large",
	http.StatusUnsupportedMediaType:  "unsupported-media-type",
	http.StatusInternalServerError:   "internal-error",
}

// Problem is the JSON an error becomes.
type Problem struct {
	Type      string              `json:"type"`
	Title     string              `json:"title"`
	Status    int                 `json:"status"`
	Detail    string              `json:"detail,omitempty"`
	Instance  string              `json:"instance"`
	RequestID string              `json:"requestId"`
	Errors    []domain.FieldError `json:"errors,omitempty"`
}

// httpError is the error for a status that needs no more explaining.
func httpError(status int, detail string) error {
	return &domain.ProblemError{Status: status, Type: byStatus[status], Detail: detail}
}
```

```go
func writeProblem(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, pe *domain.ProblemError) {
	p := Problem{
		Type: problemTypes + pe.Type, Title: titles[pe.Type], Status: pe.Status,
		Detail: pe.Detail, Instance: r.URL.Path, RequestID: RequestID(r.Context()), Errors: pe.Fields,
	}
	w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/problem+json")
	w.WriteHeader(p.Status)
	json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(p)
}
```

`titles` holds each problem type's title, in one place, so every problem of a type reads the same, and `byStatus` names the type for the plain HTTP errors. `Problem` is the JSON shape, with `omitempty` tags that leave out an empty `detail` and an empty `errors`. `httpError` builds the error for a plain HTTP failure, which part 6 explains. `writeProblem` is the only place a problem becomes a response: it adds `instance` and `requestId` from the request, and sets the header before `WriteHeader`.

examples.title: A problem, headers and all
examples.prompt: Ask for a booking that doesn't exist, and look at the headers as well as the body.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/problem+json
X-Request-Id: 4TRNSX4XIDFXYC4M4V6QBW4WDX
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:51:08 GMT
Content-Length: 204

{"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/not-found","title":"Resource not found","status":404,"detail":"booking 1999: not found","instance":"/v1/bookings/1999","requestId":"4TRNSX4XIDFXYC4M4V6QBW4WDX"}
examples.explanation: The headers say what the body is before a client reads a byte of it: `application/problem+json`. The body has the five standard members, with `not-found` as the type, the same one every 404 in Roombook uses. The detail is the error's own message, `booking 1999: not found`, which the service wrapped around the store's `ErrNotFound`, as part 6 shows. `requestId` matches the `X-Request-Id` header, so whoever reports the error can quote it.

steps.title: Central error handling

examples.title: Broken JSON
examples.prompt: Send a body that stops halfway through.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/invalid-json","title":"Body is not valid JSON","status":400,"detail":"The body couldn't be parsed as JSON.","instance":"/v1/bookings","requestId":"BNY7IVRRWH4OTME5T532A2D4BH"}
examples.explanation: The decoder hit the end of the body in the middle of an object and returned `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF`, which the decoding helper turned into the `invalid-json` problem. It's a 400, not a 422, because there's no content to judge: the server couldn't read the request at all.

examples.title: A crash, answered safely
examples.prompt: Ask for a test route whose handler fails with `connection to the database was lost`.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
Content-Type: application/problem+json
X-Request-Id: F7N4NQ6VRLPUTZ4KJFSXLJRBA3
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:51:08 GMT
Content-Length: 253

{"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/internal-error","title":"Internal server error","status":500,"detail":"Something went wrong on our side. Quote the request id if you report it.","instance":"/v1/crash","requestId":"F7N4NQ6VRLPUTZ4KJFSXLJRBA3"}
examples.explanation: The handler returned a plain error, so `toProblem` didn't recognize it, and `writeError` logged it and answered the generic `internal-error` problem, with not a word about the database. The server's terminal has one JSON line with `"level":"ERROR"`, the same request id, and the error. A panic gets the same answer, through `recoverPanics`. Anyone who reports the error can quote the id, and whoever fixes it can find the line in seconds.

examples.title: A method the route doesn't have
examples.prompt: Try to delete the list of rooms, a path that only answers GET.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
Allow: GET, HEAD
Content-Type: application/problem+json
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-Request-Id: CA5E3NM4SDSPHXPU5MYMGBQ7WO
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:51:08 GMT
Content-Length: 170

{"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/method-not-allowed","title":"Method not allowed","status":405,"instance":"/v1/rooms","requestId":"CA5E3NM4SDSPHXPU5MYMGBQ7WO"}
examples.explanation: The mux found the path but not the method, set `Allow: GET, HEAD`, and wrote its plain-text 405. `routeErrors` caught the status on its way through, saw that no pattern matched, and wrote Roombook's `method-not-allowed` problem instead. HEAD is in `Allow` because a `GET` pattern answers HEAD too. The `X-Content-Type-Options` header stayed from the mux's attempt, which does no harm.

recap:
- Every part of a request is untrusted text, so parse it at the edge into typed values, and pass only those inward.
- Go's types check kinds of values, not their meaning, so a validate method checks what actually arrives.
- A schema checks types, formats, ranges, and lengths, refuses unknown fields, and normalizes values, like times to UTC.
- Each operation gets its own schema, since create, replace, and patch need different fields.
- Query and path values are text too: convert them, give them defaults, and bound anything that costs the server work.
- Shape is checked at the edge, business rules in the service, and races in the database.
- 400 means unreadable, 422 means readable but invalid, and 409 means valid but in conflict with current data.
- Every error is a Problem Details object with a stable type, built in one central handler, and a 500 never reveals internals.
